profiles.meeting_scenario: A troubleshooting meeting at a software testing tools company investigating an unexpected regression in an internal prototype inspired by defect-aware SBST for Defects4J. For the past week, nightly experiments have shown that the defect-aware generator is no better than baseline EvoSuite on a 60-bug replay batch, even though earlier pilot runs showed gains when computation was constrained. The team needs to determine whether the problem comes from the class-level budget allocator, the method-level search guidance, the experiment harness, or a quiet mismatch in how run artifacts are being interpreted. The agenda is to review last night's run, compare it to the earlier positive pilot, identify likely sources of drift, and decide exactly what to rerun and instrument. The expected outcome is a concrete rerun plan specifying which prediction artifact to use, what budget settings to hold constant, what counts as bug detection for diagnosis, and how to reproduce the same sample for comparison.

members.name: Nina Park
members.expertise: Search-based software testing, EvoSuite internals, genetic algorithm fitness shaping, experiment orchestration
members.background: Nina has spent six years building automated Java test-generation pipelines and recently implemented the team's defect-aware extensions on top of EvoSuite for Defects4J experiments.
members.private_state: She wants to show the prototype is fundamentally sound and suspects the latest regression is due to setup drift rather than a flaw in the guidance logic; she is also under pressure to stabilize a leadership demo this month.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'tight budget,' they mean the fixed per-class search budget inside EvoSuite, because that is the level where SBST_CL should change behavior.
A 'detected bug' means a generated test that exposes the real fault in the raw search log before minimization and flaky-test filtering, since that reflects the search algorithm's capability.
The 'prediction scores' for this experiment are the frozen class-level defect probabilities from the earlier paper-style snapshot, not anything regenerated during nightly infrastructure runs.
If they 'rerun the same sample,' that implies the same 60 Defects4J bug IDs with the same RNG seeds so results are directly pairwise comparable.

members.name: Omar Haddad
members.expertise: Defect prediction pipelines, experiment reproducibility, evaluation harnesses, data versioning
members.background: Omar joined from an MLOps team and now maintains the defect-prediction models, feature generation scripts, and result dashboards that feed the defect-aware SBST pipeline.
members.private_state: He wants to protect the credibility of the prediction pipeline and quietly suspects the SBST side may be overreading noisy pilot gains; he is also trying to avoid another expensive full-cluster rerun.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'tight budget,' they mean the total wall-clock cap per Defects4J bug in the outer harness, because that is the operational resource limit leadership tracks.
A 'detected bug' means a bug represented in the final dashboard after test minimization, recompilation, and the harness's flaky-test stability check.

The 'prediction scores' in the nightly runs are whatever the current prediction service emitted after the feature-extractor patch that went out a week ago, because nightly artifacts are assumed to be refreshed.

If they 'rerun the same sample,' that means reusing the same project/version subset while allowing fresh seeds, since nightly comparisons are treated as aggregate distributions rather than paired runs.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the regression only matters under a 'tight budget' and discuss reproducing it under the same tight budget.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means 30 seconds of search time allocated per target class inside EvoSuite, where the class-level allocator changes search pressure.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a 30-second total wall-clock cap per Defects4J bug in the outer evaluation harness, including JVM startup, compilation, and post-processing.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In this project everyone casually says 'tight budget' without naming the system layer, and both meanings sound compatible because each is a real resource constraint attached to the same experiment.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both use phrases like 'bug found' and 'detection count' while comparing the baseline and defect-aware variant.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 counts any generated test that exposes the fault during search or in the first raw execution log, even if it is later discarded by minimization or flakiness filters.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 counts only bugs that survive minimization, recompilation, and the harness's stability checks and therefore appear in the final dashboard.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: They are both looking at the same nightly run and using routine internal shorthand like 'found' and 'counted'; because the post-processing pipeline is treated as standard plumbing, neither thinks to restate the counting boundary.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say they should verify whether the 'prediction scores' were wired correctly into the run.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the frozen CSV of class-level defect probabilities produced for the earlier positive pilot and stored with the experiment package.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the latest model outputs generated by the nightly prediction service after the feature-extractor patch deployed a week ago.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: There is only one casual label in use—'the prediction scores'—and both artifacts have the same schema, similar filenames, and occupy adjacent run directories, so the reference feels singular even though it is not.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to 'rerun the same sample'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to rerun 'the same sample' before making bigger changes.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 plans a paired rerun with the exact same 60 bug IDs and the same RNG seeds for baseline and guided runs to isolate setup drift.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 plans to reuse the same 60 bug IDs but let the nightly system assign fresh seeds, expecting comparison at the aggregate level rather than run-by-run pairing.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both approaches are standard experimental practice and the phrase 'same sample' usually refers only to the selected bug subset, so the seed policy remains an invisible implementation detail.

turns.inner_thought: Last night's replay is not behaving like the earlier pilot, but I still think the prototype is basically sound. The gains in the pilot showed up when EvoSuite had the fixed 30-second per-class search budget, exactly where the class-level allocator should help. I also care about bugs found in the raw search behavior, because that tells me whether guidance is surfacing the real fault at all. With the leadership demo coming up, I need this to look like setup drift or evaluation noise, not a fundamental failure in the search logic.
